intro:
The exercises in this chapter all circle one decision: when you have many small values that share a single lifecycle, who owns them and how do they refer to each other? The chapter's answer is a region. One owner holds every node; edges between nodes are indices, not pointers; and teardown is a single coarse step rather than a cascade of individual frees. Working through these solutions, you will build that machinery from the inside, starting with a bump cursor and ending with generational handles and a boundary-crossing design decision.

The through-line is that an arena is not primarily an allocation-speed trick. It is a way of making the lifetime model honest. The bump allocator gives you append-only allocation now and coarse reset later. The index AST gives you a graph with exactly one owner and no reference-cycle problem to solve. The harder exercises add scoped rewind, deletion-aware handles, and a rule for what may cross a subsystem boundary. Each builds directly on Chapter 04's borrowing rules, Chapter 06's handle design, Chapter 09's smart-pointer tradeoffs, and Chapter 10's contiguous-storage reasoning.

exerciseSolutions.title: State the bump allocator's lifetime model
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The only mutable state a bump allocator tracks across allocations is the used cursor: a single usize recording how many bytes of the fixed region have been handed out. The backing buffer itself does not change shape, and there is no free list, no per-object header, and no allocator metadata beyond that one number. This is what the chapter means by the right-hand column of the two-column model: the general heap tracks each object on its own, while the arena tracks one region and one cursor.

allocation (alloc_bytes) reads the cursor, checks that used + len does not overflow the region, copies the bytes in at the cursor, and advances the cursor to the new end. It only ever moves the cursor forward. reset sets the cursor back to zero in one step. Logically that releases the whole region's contents at once: the next allocation will overwrite from the start, so every value that lived in the region is gone together. Drop does the same thing implicitly when the arena itself goes out of scope.

There is no per-object free path because freeing one object in the middle of an append-only region would leave a hole that the cursor model cannot represent. The cursor only knows where the live high-water mark is; it has no way to record that bytes 4 through 7 are free while bytes 0 through 3 and 8 onward are live. The design deliberately trades the ability to free individual objects for the cheapness of advancing one number and the cheapness of resetting it. That is the right trade when most temporary objects share one scope: request-scoped scratch buffers, parser workspaces, the working graph a query service builds and discards per request. It is the wrong trade when individual objects must be freed independently and at different times, because the arena simply has no operation for that, and you would either leak the region until reset or be forced into a different allocator entirely.
criteria: Names the used cursor as the sole mutable state and states allocation advances it forward.
States that reset (or drop) releases the whole region in one step with no individual frees.
Ties the fit to request-scoped scratch and parser workspaces where temporaries share one scope.
Notes the weakness: poor when objects must be freed independently at different times.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace evaluation through the index-arena AST
exerciseSolutions.solution:
alloc pushes onto the nodes vector and returns ExprId(self.nodes.len()) captured before the push, so each id is the slot index the node lands in. The five allocations therefore issue ids in slot order: Number(2) -> ExprId(0) bound to two, Number(3) -> ExprId(1) bound to three, Number(4) -> ExprId(2) bound to four, Add(two, three) -> ExprId(3) bound to sum, and Mul(sum, four) -> ExprId(4) bound to root.

eval(root) looks up slot 4, finds Mul(sum, four), and recurses. eval(sum) looks up slot 3, finds Add(two, three), and recurses again: eval(two) reads slot 0 and returns 2, eval(three) reads slot 1 and returns 3, so the Add yields 2 + 3 = 5. Back in the Mul, eval(four) reads slot 2 and returns 4, so the Mul yields 5 * 4 = 20. Each recursive step reborrows from the arena root through get, because every variant holds ExprId values rather than owned children, so the recursion always indexes back into the one owning vector. The program prints value = 20 and nodes = 5.

If Add held Box<Expr> instead of ExprId, each node would own its children directly: the tree would become a chain of heap allocations, eval would match on owned sub-Exprs without consulting the arena, and len would no longer report a flat node count because there would be no flat table. The ExprId version keeps logical identity into a single owning vector, so an edge is an index, not an owner. That is the distinction the chapter draws: ExprId is identity, not shared ownership, which is exactly why this graph has one owner and no reference-cycle problem to solve.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Hand-trace of eval(root) over the five issued ExprId slots.
criteria: Maps two->0, three->1, four->2, sum->3, root->4 as the issued ids.
Trace shows eval(root) = eval(sum) * eval(four) = (2 + 3) * 4 = 20.
Reports value = 20 and nodes = 5 as the printed output.

Explains ExprId is logical identity into one owning vector, so edges are indices not owners, and states that switching Add to Box<Expr> would make each node own its children exclusively, preventing sub-expression sharing and giving a tree-only (not DAG) structure.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add a checkpoint-and-rewind API to the bump allocator
exerciseSolutions.solution:
mark and rewind are the same one-cursor idea as reset, generalized from "back to zero" to "back to a saved position." mark takes &self and returns self.used without touching any state; it is just a snapshot of the high-water mark. rewind takes &mut self and sets self.used back to the saved value, so all bytes above that point become available again for the next allocation. No individual allocation is ever freed, and allocation stays append-only above whatever the cursor currently is.

The subtle case is what rewind does when the supplied mark is greater than the current used, which would happen if a caller saved a mark, rewound past it once, and then tried to rewind to the stale higher mark again. Moving the cursor forward to an arbitrary mark would expose stale bytes that were logically released and may have been overwritten or never written, so the implementation treats a forward rewind as a misuse. It guards the case with a debug assertion and clamps in release builds so the cursor never moves forward through rewind. This keeps the invariant that rewind only ever reclaims space, matching the chapter's framing that the cursor moves forward only on allocation and backward only on reset or rewind.

The test allocates one value, marks, allocates two more, then rewinds to the mark and confirms used returns to the marked value. A subsequent alloc_bytes then writes over the reclaimed region, demonstrating the bytes were genuinely reused rather than freed.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: mark/rewind reuse the one-cursor model, guarding the unsound forward case.
criteria: mark has signature fn mark(&self) -> usize and returns self.used without mutation.
rewind sets self.used to the mark so later allocations reuse the region above it.
No individual allocation is freed; allocation stays append-only above the cursor.
The test allocates, marks, allocates more, rewinds, and used returns to the marked value.

exerciseSolutions.title: Add deletion-aware handles to the AST arena
exerciseSolutions.solution:
A plain usize index cannot tell whether the slot it points at still holds the node it was issued for. Once a slot is removed and reused, the old index silently reads the new occupant. The fix is a generational handle: each slot stores a generation counter plus an Option<Expr>, and ExprId carries the (index, generation) pair it was issued for. A read is valid only when the index is in range, the slot is occupied, and the handle's generation equals the slot's current generation.

remove clears the slot's value to None and bumps its generation. That single increment is what invalidates every handle previously issued for that slot, because their stored generation now differs from the slot's current generation. alloc prefers a free slot from a free list; when it reuses a slot it leaves the already-bumped generation in place and stores the new value, so the new handle is issued with the new generation. A stale handle to the old occupant still carries the pre-bump generation, so its get returns None, while a fresh handle to the reused slot matches and returns the new node.

This is the generational arena the chapter describes: the generation counter exists precisely to distinguish a slot's old occupant from its new one. It turns a use-after-free-shaped bug, reading a stale index into a reused slot, into a clean Option::None at the read site, with the cost of one extra usize per slot and one comparison per access. eval is updated to expect a live handle and unwrap through get, since evaluation only ever runs over a tree of currently-live nodes.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Generational (index, generation) handles reject access to a reused slot.
criteria: ExprId carries both an index and a generation rather than a bare usize.
remove bumps the slot's generation so previously issued handles no longer match.
get returns None when the handle's generation differs from the slot's current generation.
A reused slot serves new handles correctly while the stale old handle returns None.

exerciseSolutions.title: Remove the reference cycle from an Rc graph
exerciseSolutions.solution:
In the Rc version every edge is an Rc<Node> owner, so each edge contributes a strong count to its target. The back-edge from D to A means A is kept alive by D, and following the forward edges A keeps D alive transitively. That forms a cycle of strong references: A's strong count never falls to zero because D holds it, and D's never falls to zero because the chain from A reaches it. When the external handles go out of scope, the cycle's internal counts remain at least one, so none of the nodes in the cycle are ever dropped. That is the leak. RefCell does not cause it; it only enables the mutation that lets you install the back-edge. The leak is purely the ownership cycle in the strong counts.

The repair the chapter prescribes is structural, not a patch: make one arena own every node in a single vector, and make every edge a NodeId index into that vector instead of an Rc<Node>. Now there is exactly one owner, the arena's nodes vector. Edges own nothing; a NodeId is a plain Copy value that confers no ownership and bumps no count. You build the graph by allocating each node and connecting them by handle, including the D-to-A back-edge, which is now just the index of A stored in D.

The identical back-edge no longer leaks because indices are not owners. A NodeId being stored in D's edge list does not keep A's storage alive; A is kept alive solely by the arena, and exactly as long as the arena. When the arena drops, the whole region drops together in one step, cycles and all, because dropping a Vec<Node> of plain index-bearing nodes never has to chase a pointer or decrement a foreign count. You removed the cycle by construction rather than by retrofitting Weak references after the fact. This is the same one-owner-plus-handles shape the chapter recommends for ASTs, IR, routing graphs, and domain DAGs.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Arena-and-index graph: one owner, indices for edges, back-edge cannot leak.
criteria: Explains that Rc edges are owners, so the cycle keeps strong counts above zero and nodes never drop.
The refactored graph has exactly one owner: the arena vector of nodes.
Every edge stores a NodeId index rather than an Rc or Box, so edges own nothing.
States the cycle is removed by construction because indices are not owners and the region drops together.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose between borrowed-reference and index arenas at a boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The two arena styles differ in what crosses the boundary back to the caller. A reference arena hands back &'arena T: a borrow chained to the arena's lifetime. An index arena hands back a small owned handle such as ExprId or NodeId that owns nothing and is Copy. That difference is the whole decision, because the borrow checker treats them oppositely at a boundary.

The borrow checker forbids the arena-borrowed reference from outliving the arena. Its lifetime is tied to the arena's, so you cannot store it in a cache that outlives the request, and you cannot move it into an async task whose future may be polled after the request scope ends. The compiler rejects both at the point you try, which is exactly the protection you want, but it means a reference arena cannot serve data that crosses a long-lived boundary. The owned handle has no such tie: it is a plain value, so it travels freely across async tasks, queues, and caches.

For this query service I keep arena-borrowed references for the phase-local synchronous work, name resolution, plan construction, and analysis passes that run entirely within the request and discard the working graph at the end. What crosses to the cache and to the async task is owned data: either fully owned values copied out of the arena (a resolved plan, a result row) or stable handles paired with the arena or table they index into, kept alive for as long as the consumer needs them. The async task that may outlive the request must not hold an arena borrow; it gets owned values or a handle into a structure with an independent, longer lifetime.

The chapter says to ask three questions before picking a style. First, do I want arena-tied references or handles? References are strongest when the phase stays local and synchronous; handles when data must travel. Second, do I need deletion? If slots are removed and reused, a bare index is unsafe and you need a generational handle. Third, does stale-handle protection matter? If a consumer can hold a handle across a removal, you need the generation check to turn stale access into None rather than a silent wrong read. For a boundary-crossing cache, the answers point to stable, generation-checked handles for anything retained, and arena references confined to the synchronous request phase.
criteria: States a reference arena returns a borrow tied to the arena's lifetime, forbidden from outliving it.
States an index arena returns a small owned handle that can travel across async tasks, queues, and caches.
Keeps arena references for phase-local synchronous work and uses owned values or stable handles across boundaries.
Lists the three questions: reference vs handle, deletion needed, and stale-handle protection.

labSolution.expectedOutput:
used = 9
a = query
b = plan
overflow = true
after reset = 0
c = next
labSolution.explanation:
alloc_bytes is the whole exercise. It computes end = used + len with checked_add so an absurd length cannot wrap, rejects the request with None when end exceeds the region size N, and otherwise copies the bytes in at the current cursor, advances used to end, and returns the (start, end) range. Allocation only ever moves the cursor forward; it never frees.

In main, the region is Bump::<16>. Allocating b"query" (5 bytes) takes used from 0 to 5 and returns (0, 5). Allocating b"plan" (4 bytes) takes used to 9 and returns (5, 9), so used = 9 prints, and slicing each range back through slice yields query and plan. b"too-many-bytes" is 14 bytes; 9 + 14 = 23 exceeds 16, so alloc_bytes returns None and overflow.is_none() is true. reset sets used back to 0 in one coarse step, releasing the whole region logically, so after reset = 0. The final b"next" allocates from the start of the now-empty region and prints next. The printed lines match the expected output exactly.

The lab's lesson is the lifetime model rather than the arithmetic: append-only allocation now, single overflow guard at the boundary, and one cheap reset that discards everything at once with no per-object free path.

reviewAnswers.question: What single piece of mutable state does a bump allocator maintain, and what do allocation and reset each do to it?
reviewAnswers.answer: It maintains a single used cursor: the count of bytes already handed out of the fixed region. Allocation checks for overflow, copies the bytes in at the cursor, and advances the cursor forward by the allocation size. Reset sets the cursor back to zero in one step, logically releasing the whole region's contents at once, with no per-object free path anywhere in the type.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does an arena-and-index AST avoid the reference-cycle problem that an Rc<RefCell<Node>> graph can hit?
reviewAnswers.answer: In an Rc graph every edge is an owner, so a cycle of edges keeps the involved strong counts above zero and those nodes are never dropped. In an arena-and-index AST there is exactly one owner, the arena's vector, and every edge is just an ExprId or NodeId index that owns nothing and changes no reference count. Because indices are not owners, a back-edge cannot keep anything alive, so cycles are removed by construction and the entire region drops together when the arena drops.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the difference between what a reference arena and an index arena hand back across a boundary, and which one the borrow checker ties to the arena's lifetime?
reviewAnswers.answer: A reference arena hands back a borrow that is chained to the arena's lifetime, and the borrow checker forbids that reference from outliving the arena, so it cannot be stored in a longer-lived cache or moved into an async task that may outlive the request. An index arena hands back a small owned handle that owns nothing and is Copy, so it can travel freely across async tasks, queues, and caches. The borrow checker ties only the reference arena's output to the arena's lifetime; the handle carries no such tie.

reviewAnswers.question: What problem does a generation counter on an arena handle solve that a plain usize index does not?
reviewAnswers.answer: A plain usize index keeps pointing at a slot after that slot is removed and reused, so it silently reads whatever new value now occupies the slot, a stale-access bug. A generation counter records, per slot, how many times it has been reused, and the handle stores the generation it was issued for; removing a node bumps the slot's generation. On read, comparing the handle's generation against the slot's current generation returns None for any stale handle, turning a silent wrong read into a clean failure at the access site.

reviewAnswers.question: The arena's only cheap teardown operation is whole-region reset, not per-object free. When does that make it the wrong fit?
reviewAnswers.answer: It is the wrong fit when objects have independent, staggered lifetimes and must be freed individually at different times, because the bump model has no per-object free operation and can only reclaim space by resetting or dropping the whole region. If the workload does not actually share one region lifetime, the arena either forces you to hold memory until reset or pushes you toward a different allocator, and the lifetime mismatch eventually shows. The arena pays off only when most temporaries genuinely share one scope, such as request-scoped scratch or parser workspaces.

reviewAnswers.question: Given the chapter's three-question framework, which crate family fits a build-once AST and which fits a deleting registry that needs stale-handle protection?
reviewAnswers.answer: A build-once AST answers the framework with references-or-handles but no deletion and no stale-handle concern, because the tree is parsed once, traversed many times, and discarded whole. That points at typed-arena when you want arena-tied references chained to the arena's lifetime, or id-arena when you prefer stable typed handles that travel more easily; bumpalo fits when you only need fast region allocation underneath. A deleting registry answers the framework differently: it needs deletion and slot reuse, and a bare index becomes unsafe the moment a slot is reused, so it needs stale-handle protection. That points at generational-arena or slotmap, where the handle carries an index plus a generation so a reused slot rejects old handles, with slab as the choice when you want fast slot reuse and stable handles without the region-teardown framing.
